terms.meaning: the code lines a beat can be measured on, with blank lines and wrapper lines removed
the name of the first block of a cycle, used as one label for the whole cycle
one group of blocks that call each other in a cycle, held as a single node
one text of the map tree, known by an id like F03 or F14.3
one small piece of the file, a list of line ranges that a beat can hold
the lines of a node that no statement inside it covers, such as an if header or an else line
a node of the tree that has no children
a function that the block calls

map.name: script
map.takes: nothing but the module load
map.gives: the module-level names PROMPT and CALLS, and the run of main()
map.story:
Example: `python decompile.py decompile.py` writes map.json in the same folder.
PROMPT is a template, so its literal JSON braces are doubled and PROMPT.format leaves them as single braces.
An import of this file runs nothing; only the command line starts main().
map.text: script — sets up the imports, the prompt template and the call counter, then runs main() when the file is started from the command line

children.text:
Bring in the tools the compiler needs:

ast — reads the python file as a tree, so blocks, statements and calls can be found.
json — reads the model answer and writes map.json.
re — regular expressions.
subprocess — starts the claude command.
sys — gives the command line arguments and stops the run on failure.
Path — holds the file path and reads and writes text.

jedi — finds where each name is defined and where it is used, for the links between texts.

PROMPT = the full instruction text sent to the model for one block.

It holds the file, the block label and its line spans, the cells, the statement ranges, the beat rules, the root rules, the story rules, a gold example and the JSON shape of the answer.
It is a template: the fields in braces are filled in later, and the braces that must stay in the text are doubled.

CALLS = a one-item list that counts the calls to the model.

A list, not a number, so ask_claude can add to it from inside its own function and the final report can print the total.
When the file is started as a program, and not imported, call main() to read the file named on the command line and write map.json beside it.

map.name: statements
map.takes: a file path and its source text
map.gives: one row per statement, in tree order
map.story:
Example: for the source "def f():\n    return 1", statements gives [(0, 1, 2), (1, 2, 2)].
The def row and the return row both appear, the parent before the statement inside it.
The first number is the depth, so nesting stays visible.
When path does not end in .py, the result is an empty list.
map.text: statements(path, src) -> list of (depth, first line, last line) — lists every statement of a Python file with the line range it holds and how deep it sits

children.text: statements(path, src) takes the path of one file and the source text of that file.

Stop at once when the file is not Python.
Only Python source parses into a tree here, so any other suffix gives an empty list.
rows = the list of statement records, empty at the start.
Parse src into a tree, then let walk record every statement under it from depth 0, and give rows back to the caller.

map.name: statements.walk
map.takes: an AST node and the nesting depth of its statements
map.gives: nothing; it appends rows to the rows list outside it
map.story:
Example: for a def on lines 51-65 that holds one if, walk(the module, 0) appends (0, 51, 65), then (1, 52, 53).
A node that is not a statement adds no row, but walk still looks inside it at the same depth.
So an if test that holds a lambda keeps the depth of its own body.
map.text: walk(node, depth) -> None — records every statement under a node as (depth, first line, last line) and goes down into it

children.text: walk(node, depth) looks at each direct child of node, one at a time

when the child is a statement, add one row to rows: the depth, the first line, and the last line.
Then walk the child at depth + 1, because everything inside a statement is one level deeper.

when the child is not a statement, add no row and walk it at the same depth.
This keeps the depth counted in statements only, not in every AST node between them.

map.name: cells_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the cells of the file, in line order
map.story:
Example: line 5 holds a comment, and def f() runs from line 6 to line 7.
cells_of gives one cell for lines 5-7, because the comment joins the def under it.
Blank lines go in no cell. A leftover run after the last cell joins that last cell. In a file that is not Python, each run of non-blank lines is one cell.
map.text: cells_of(path, src, lines) -> list of cells — cuts the file into cells, one line range each, so every non-blank line sits in exactly one cell

children.text:
spans = the line ranges found so far, one [start, end] pair each.
cells_of fills it, and the branch below runs only when the file is a .py file.

Parse the source and call emit on each top-level statement.
emit adds to spans the line runs that no statement inside it owns, and repeats on those inner statements.

When spans is still empty — the file is not Python, or the file has no statements — use the blank lines instead.
Each run of non-blank lines becomes one cell, and cells_of returns those cells here.

Prepare the search for lines that no statement holds:

covered = every line number the spans already hold
extra = the leftover runs, collected below
a = the first line of the run being built, or None

Read the lines in order and collect each run of non-blank lines that covered misses.
Comments make most of these runs, because the parser puts no comment in a statement.
A run still open at the last line closes there.

Give each leftover run to the first span that starts after it: that span's start moves back to the start of the run.
When no span comes after the run, the last span extends to the end of the run.
Return the spans in line order, each one as a cell.

map.name: cells_of.kids_of
map.takes: one ast node
map.gives: its nearest statement children, in source order
map.story:
Example: kids_of on the for node at lines 73-77 gives one node, the if node at 74-77.
The body of that if node is not returned. kids_of looks through a child that is not a statement, like a test expression. A node with no statement under it gives an empty list.
map.text: kids_of(node) -> list of ast statement nodes — finds the nearest statement nodes under one node, without going inside those statements

children.text:
out = the statement nodes found under node

It starts empty and fills as each child is checked.
step over every direct child of node, in source order

A child that is a statement goes into out, and the search stops there: the lines inside that statement are not opened.
A child that is not a statement — a test expression, a decorator, an argument list — is opened by kids_of itself, and the statements it finds inside join out.
give the caller the one layer of statements that was found

map.name: cells_of.emit
map.takes: one ast statement node
map.gives: nothing; it appends the new spans to the shared spans list
map.story:
Example: node covers lines 1-4, with `if c:` on line 1 and `else:` on line 3.
emit adds [2,2] and [4,4] for the two bodies, then [1,1] and [3,3] for the own lines.
A node with no statement inside it gives one span for all of its lines.
Blank lines never enter a span.
Each child adds its spans before the parent adds its own lines.
map.text: emit(node) -> None — adds to spans the line runs of node that no statement inside it owns, and calls itself on each of those inner statements

children.text:
kids = the statement nodes that sit directly inside node, from kids_of

emit needs them to know which lines of node belong to a child and which belong to node itself.

When node has no statement inside it, all of its lines become one span and emit stops here.
This is the simple case: an assignment or a call owns every line of its own range.

covered = every line number that a child statement uses

In the same loop emit calls itself on each child, so each child puts its own spans in first.

Read the lines of node from first to last and keep the runs of lines that are not in covered and are not blank.
Each run that ends becomes one span. A run ends at the first line that a child uses or that is empty.
This is why one header can give more than one span: the if line and the else line are two runs.
When a run is still open at the last line, close it at node.end_lineno and add that final span.

map.name: merge
map.takes: a list of line ranges
map.gives: the joined ranges, sorted and separate
map.story:
Example: merge([[5, 6], [1, 2], [3, 4]]) gives [[1, 6]].
Spans that only touch join, because [1, 2] ends one line before [3, 4] starts.
A real gap keeps them apart: [[1, 2], [4, 5]] stays two ranges.
The input order does not matter, and one span may swallow a shorter one inside it.
map.text: merge(spans) -> list of line ranges — joins the spans that overlap or touch into one span each, in line order

children.text:
out = the joined ranges so far, empty at the start

Each new span is compared only against the last range in out, so the input must be sorted first.

Walk the spans from the lowest start to the highest.
When the new span starts at or before one line past the end of the last range, it overlaps or touches it: push that end out to the later of the two ends.
When it starts further along, a real gap sits between them, so add it to out as a range of its own.
Give back the joined ranges.

map.name: ask_claude
map.takes: a prompt string
map.gives: the parsed JSON object from the model answer
map.story:
Example: claude answers Sure: {"a": 1} thanks. ask_claude gives {"a": 1}.
Text before the first { and after the last } is dropped.
A non-zero exit stops the run and shows the last 500 characters of stderr.
The command has 600 seconds to answer.
map.text: ask_claude(prompt) -> dict — sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and gives back the JSON object in the answer

children.text:
count this call in CALLS

CALLS = a one-slot list that counts every claude call of the run.
main prints that count at the end, so the reader sees the price of a compile.

run the claude command with the prompt and ask it for JSON output, then stop the program when the command fails.
The error message keeps the last 500 characters of stderr, enough to see the cause.

read the answer text out of the command JSON, then cut from its first { to its last } and parse that piece.
The cut removes any words the model wrote around the object.

map.name: check_block
map.takes: a model answer plus the cells, statements and code lines it must fit
map.gives: the four checked parts of the answer
map.story:
Example: with 3 cells, beats 1-2 then 3-3 pass; beats 1-2 then 2-3 fail.
The first broken rule raises AssertionError with a message that names the beat.
A beat holds a whole statement or only lines inside one, never a part of it.
Only the lines in ess count in that test.
map.text: check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) -> root, story, terms, beats — checks one model answer against every rule and fails on the first break

children.text:
root = the signature part of the answer, which must be a dictionary
It needs text, takes and gives, each one a string with characters in it.
when label names a function, root text must start with that name and an open bracket, so the signature belongs to the block it explains
story = the explanation a person reads, which must be a string with characters in it

terms = the words the story defines, and an empty list is legal
Each term needs a term string and a meaning string.
The term must also appear word for word in the story, so no definition is given for a word the reader never sees.

beats = the steps of the explanation, which must be a list with at least one step

at = the cell number the next beat must start at, set to 1 before the walk

walk the beats in order and check each one against three rules:
a == at — the beat starts one cell after the beat before it
a <= b <= len(cells) — the end is not before the start and not past the last cell
text — the step is a string with words in it

got = every file line the beat's cells cover, kept down to the lines in ess
Blank lines and wrapper lines are dropped, because a beat can not cut them.

compare got with every statement of the block: the beat must hold all of the statement, or only lines inside it, or none of them
When it holds a part of one and something outside it, the message lists the cells inside that statement, so the model can repair the beat.

Then at moves to the cell after this beat.

the last beat must end at the last cell, so the beats cover all of them
Then give root, story, terms and beats back to the caller.

map.name: carve
map.takes: a first and last line number, ranges to remove, and the file lines
map.gives: the free line ranges in order
map.story:
Example: carve(1, 5, [[3, 3]], lines) with line 2 blank gives [[1, 1], [4, 5]].
minus covers line 3, so the result skips it. The result trims blank lines from the ends of each range. A range of only blank lines does not appear.
map.text: carve(a, b, minus, lines) -> list of line ranges — returns the parts of a..b that no minus range covers, with blank lines trimmed off each end

children.text:
Set up the walk over the lines from a to b:

used = every line number that a range in minus covers
spans = the free runs found up to now
run = the first line of the run now open, or None when no run is open

Step over each line from a to b, and one step past b.
A line is free when it is not larger than b and not in used.
The first free line opens a run; the first line that is not free closes the run into spans.
The extra step past b closes a run that touches the end.

Trim each span: move its start forward over blank lines, and move its end backward over blank lines.
A span with only blank lines becomes empty and is not kept.
This keeps the empty lines between two functions out of both results.
Give the trimmed ranges back to the caller.

map.name: blocks_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text and its lines
map.gives: one record per block, with its name, its line ranges and its node
map.story:
Example: a file with imports on lines 1-2, def f on lines 3-8, and a nested def g on lines 5-6.
blocks_of gives f with lines 3-4 and 7-8, f.g with lines 5-6, and script with lines 1-2.
A nested def keeps the dotted name f.g, and its lines leave the parent block.
The script block appears only when a line sits outside every def.
For a file that is not Python, all the lines become the one script block.
map.text: blocks_of(path, src, lines) -> list of blocks — splits the file into one block per def or class, plus a script block for the lines outside them

children.text:
fns = the list of every def and class in the file, empty until the file is read

Only a .py file is parsed, so any other file keeps this list empty.
grab() reads the parsed file and puts one record in fns for each def and class: its dotted name, its first and last line, and its node.

blocks = one record per def or class, holding the lines that def owns alone

For each def f, inner collects the spans of the defs nested inside it, and carve() gives back the parts of f that no nested def covers. A nested def is a block of its own, so its parent must not claim those lines twice.

out = the lines of the file that no def covers, from carve() over line 1 to the last line

These leftover lines become the block named script. When nothing is left, no script block is added.
sort the blocks by their first line, so the caller reads them in file order, then hand them back.

map.name: blocks_of.grab
map.takes: an AST node and the names of the defs around it
map.gives: no value; it appends one record per def to fns
map.story:
Example: on this file grab records blocks_of, then enters it and records blocks_of.grab.
The inner name keeps the outer name in front of it, joined with a dot.
A decorated def starts at its first decorator line, not at its def line.
A def written inside an if or a for is found too.
map.text: grab(node, scope) -> nothing — records every def and class under node into fns, with its dotted name, its line span and its node

children.text:
grab(node, scope) looks at the direct children of node, one child at a time.
scope = the names of the defs already entered, outermost first.

When the child is a function or a class, keep a record of it in fns:
name: the child name with scope in front of it, joined by dots
span: the first line, which is the first decorator line when the child has decorators, to the last line
node: the child itself, for later work

Then grab enters that child with its name added to scope, so a def inside it gets the longer name.
Any other child is not a def, but a def can be inside it, so grab looks in it with the same scope.

map.name: calls_of
map.takes: one block, the top-level syntax nodes of the file, and the set of all block names
map.gives: the names of the blocks it calls, in sorted order
map.story:
Example: calls_of uses the name scan, so the result is ["calls_of.scan"].
A nested helper comes back under its dotted name, found by trying the scope path outward.
Names inside nested defs are skipped, and a block never lists itself.
map.text: calls_of(block, body, names) -> sorted list of block names — reports which other blocks this one block uses, so the caller can order the blocks by their calls

children.text:
Three things get ready before the walk:

skip = the syntax node types of a def or a class, because those lines belong to their own block
scope = the parts of this block's dotted name, empty for the script block
out = the set that collects the names this block calls

Run scan over the right nodes: a function block scans its own node, the script block scans every top-level node that is not a def or a class.
scan walks everything under a node and puts each name that points at another block into out.
Hand back the collected names in sorted order, so the list is the same on every run.

map.name: calls_of.resolve
map.takes: a bare name used inside the block
map.gives: the matching dotted block name, or None
map.story:
Example: inside calls_of, resolve("scan") gives "calls_of.scan", but resolve("merge") gives "merge".
The search starts at the deepest scope and steps out one level each turn.
The first candidate that is in names wins, so a nested function hides a top-level one.
A word that no block defines gives None.
map.text: resolve(word) -> a block name or None — turns a bare name written in the code into the full dotted name of the block it points at

children.text:
word = the bare name as the code writes it, with no dots

The block reads two things it does not take as arguments:
scope — the dotted path of the block being scanned
names — the set of dotted names of all blocks in the file

try the scope from the inside out: for each cut k, join scope[:k] with word and keep the first joined name that is in names.
The first turn keeps the whole scope, so a name defined next to the caller is found before an outer one with the same word.
when no cut of the scope makes a known name, give None, because the word points at an import, a builtin, or a local variable, not at a block of this file

map.name: calls_of.scan
map.takes: one node of the syntax tree
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out set
map.story:
Example: scan meets the line stmts = statements(path, src) and out gains "statements".
A def or a class under node is not entered, so the names inside it never count.
A name that is not a block, like ast or path, is dropped. The block's own name is dropped too.
map.text: scan(node) -> None — walks everything under one syntax node and puts every name that points at another block into out

children.text: scan takes one node and reads the code under it, one child at a time
step over each direct child c of the node

when the child is a def or a class, leave it alone.
skip holds the three node types that start a block of their own, and the names inside them belong to that block's story, not to this one.

when the child is a plain name, ask resolve which block the bare name c.id points at.

hit = that block name, or None when the name is not a block at all.
Add hit to out, but never when it equals block["name"], because a block calling itself is not a call out.
call scan on the child, so names further down inside the same block are found too

map.name: layers_of
map.takes: the blocks and the call names of each block
map.gives: a layer number for each block name
map.story:
Example: main calls compile_block, and compile_block calls ask_claude.
Then layers_of gives ask_claude 1, compile_block 2, and main 3.
Blocks that call each other in a cycle share one layer number.
A block that calls nothing gets layer 1.
map.text: layers_of(blocks, calls) -> dict from block name to int — gives every block a layer number, so a block always sits above the blocks it calls

children.text:
Set up the record books for the Tarjan search:

idx = the order number each block name got when the search first reached it
low = the smallest order number each block name can still reach
on = the block names now on the working stack
st = the working stack itself
comp = the component id of each block name

k = a one-slot list that holds the next order number
A list is used, not a plain number, so the inner search can raise it.
Run strong() on every block name the search has not reached yet, which fills comp with a shared id for each group of blocks that call each other in a cycle.

edges = the calls between components, one set of callee components per caller component
Calls inside one component are dropped, so what is left has no cycles and can be measured by depth.

h = the layer number already worked out for each component
height() reads and fills this, so no component is measured twice.
Ask height() for the layer of each block's component, and give back the name-to-layer answer.

map.name: layers_of.strong
map.takes: a block name
map.gives: comp entries for v and the blocks below it
map.story:
Example: calls has f calling g and g calling f; strong("f") sets comp["f"] and comp["g"] to "f".
A block in no cycle gets its own name as its component id. Every name is visited once, so a second strong(v) on the same name never runs.
map.text: strong(v) -> None — runs one Tarjan search from block name v and writes a shared component id into comp for every block in v's call cycle

children.text:
number v as it is first seen:

idx[v] = the visit number of v, taken from the counter k[0], which then moves on.
low[v] = the lowest visit number v can reach; it starts equal to idx[v].

v also goes on the stack st and into the set on, so the walk below can tell that v is still open.

walk every block that v calls.

A callee not numbered yet: strong goes into it first, then v takes the lower of the two low values.
A callee still in on: v drops low[v] to that callee's visit number, because v and the callee sit in one cycle.

when low[v] came back equal to idx[v], nothing v reaches is older than v, so v is the first block of its cycle.
Pop st down to v and set comp[w] = v for each block popped, which gives the whole cycle one name.

map.name: layers_of.height
map.takes: a component key
map.gives: its layer number
map.story:
Example: c calls d, and d calls nothing.
Then height(d) gives 1, and height(c) gives 2.
A component that calls nothing gets the layer 1. The dict h keeps each answer, so one component is counted one time. A cycle cannot occur here, because layers_of put each cycle into one component first.
map.text: height(c) -> int — gives the layer number of one component: 1 more than the largest layer among the components it calls

children.text:
h[c] = the layer number of the component c.
The dict h holds it, so the work is done one time for each component.

height calls itself on every component in edges.get(c, ()), takes the largest answer, and adds 1.
A component with no edges gives an empty tuple to max, which then uses default=0, so the layer is 1.
give back the stored layer number of c

map.name: nodes_of
map.takes: a list of root nodes, each with optional children
map.gives: every node in the tree as a flat list
map.story:
Example: a tree of one root with two children gives a list of 3 nodes.
Parents come before their children, and each root finishes before the next starts.
The nodes are the same dicts, not copies. An empty tree gives an empty list.
map.text: nodes_of(tree) -> flat list of nodes — collects every node of a map tree, roots and all descendants, into one list

children.text: out = the flat list of nodes, empty at the start
walk(tree) adds every root and everything below it to out
give the full flat list back

map.name: nodes_of.walk
map.takes: a list of node dicts
map.gives: nothing back; the out list grows
map.story:
Example: ns is one node F01 that has one child F01.1.
walk(ns) appends F01 first, then F01.1, to out.
A parent always goes in before its children. A node with no children ends that branch. walk returns nothing; it only fills out.
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — adds every node in ns, and everything below it, to the out list of nodes_of

children.text:
take ns, a list of nodes

ns is the top of the tree on the first call, and the children of one node on every deeper call
read the nodes in order and append each one to out, so a node is recorded before anything under it

when a node has a children list, walk calls itself on that list, so the nodes below it join out too

a node with no children stops the descent there

map.name: number
map.takes: the list of top-level block nodes
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id field into every node
map.story:
Example: the first block gets id "F01", and its three beats get "F01.1", "F01.2", "F01.3".
The counter for beats restarts at 1 inside each top-level block.
A block with no children keeps only its own id.
The tree is changed in place, so nothing is returned.
map.text: number(tree) -> None — gives every node in the map tree a stable id, F01 for the first top-level block and F01.1, F01.2 for its beats

children.text:
number(tree) walks the top-level blocks in order and writes each one an id like F01, F02, F03.
The two digits keep the ids sorted the same way as text and as numbers.

k = the count of beats numbered inside the current block.
It starts at 0 for every block, so beat numbers are local to their block.

walk(t.get("children") or []) then stamps every beat under this block with an id like F01.1. A block with no children passes an empty list, so nothing more happens.

map.name: number.walk
map.takes: a list of child nodes
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id field into each node it reaches
map.story:
Example: t is F01 with two children, and the first child has one child of its own.
walk sets F01.1 on the first child, F01.2 on that grandchild, then F01.3 on the second child.
The counter k never restarts at a deeper level, so the number does not show depth.
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — walks the child nodes under one top-level tree node and stamps a numbered id on every one of them

children.text: walk takes ns, a list of nodes, and looks at each node c in turn

count one more node, then name it

k[0] = how many nodes walk has reached so far under this top-level node t
c["id"] = the id of t, a dot, and that count, like F01.3

when c has children of its own, walk calls itself on c["children"]
the same k counter continues there, so every node deep in the tree gets its own number

map.name: owner_of
map.takes: a numbered map tree
map.gives: a table from line number to node id
map.story:
Example: F01 has children F01.1 on lines 1-2 and F01.2 on line 3.
owner_of gives {1: "F01.1", 2: "F01.1", 3: "F01.2"}.
Only a leaf claims lines, so the parent F01 is not in the table. A line that no leaf covers has no entry.
map.text: owner_of(tree) -> dict from line number to node id — says which text of the map owns each line of the file

children.text: owner = an empty table from a line number to the id of the node that owns it

walk every node of the tree with nodes_of, and keep only the nodes with no children

for each of those, write its id against every line number of every span it holds, so the deepest text of the tree owns the line
give the finished table back

map.name: links
map.takes: a Python file path and a map from line number to node id
map.gives: one row per shared name, with the node that defines it and the nodes that use it
map.story:
Example: owner puts line 135 in node F03 and line 420 in node F14.3.
The name merge, defined on line 135, gives one row: name merge, def F03, used F14.3.
A name used only inside its own node gives no row. Imported names like ast are skipped, because they are defined in another file. A file that is not Python gives an empty list.
map.text: links(path, owner) -> list of rows — finds every name defined in this file and reports which other map nodes use it

children.text:
Stop early for a file that is not Python.

jedi reads Python only, so any other suffix gives an empty list at once.

Prepare the three things the scan needs:

p = the absolute path of the file, used later to test where a name is defined.
script = the jedi reader of that file, which lists the names and their uses.
rows = the results collected so far, empty at the start.

Go through each name jedi finds in the file and remove the ones that do not count.

A name whose definition is in another module is an import, so skip it.
src = the id of the node that holds the definition line, taken from owner.
When owner has no node for that line, skip the name too.

used = the ids of the other nodes that mention this name, sorted and without repeats.

The node of the definition itself is removed, so only uses that cross a node border stay.
Keep the name only when at least one other node uses it.
Give rows back, one entry for each name that is used outside the node that defines it.

map.name: row_of
map.takes: a cell number, a cell, and the file lines
map.gives: one text line that names the cell in the prompt
map.story:
Example: cell 4 covers lines 90-92 and 95-96, and line 90 is "for n in range(10):".
row_of gives "4: lines 90-92, 95-96 | for n in range(10):".
A cell with many spans shows all of them, but only one line of code.
That code line is always the first line of the first span.
map.text: row_of(i, c, lines) -> string — writes one cell as a numbered prompt line: its index, its line ranges, and its first line of code

children.text:
spans = the cell's line ranges as text, like "90-92, 95-96"
The reader of the prompt needs to see every range the cell holds, not only the first.

build the finished line: the cell number, then the spans, then the first line of code from the file, trimmed of its indent.
This line goes into the prompt so the model can point at a cell by number.

map.name: write_node
map.takes: a map node and the indent to put before it
map.gives: the node as JSON text, its children nested below it
map.story:
Example: a node with id F01.1, layer 1, no name key and no children, at indent "  ".
Result: one line after two spaces, {"id": "F01.1", "layer": 1, "text": ..., "lines": ...}.
A node with a name key also gets name, calls, takes, gives, and story when it has one.
Children come from write_node itself, with two more spaces of indent.
Each node keeps to one line, however long its text.
map.text: write_node(t, ind) -> a line of JSON text — writes one map node, and every node under it, as indented JSON text

children.text:
head = the JSON text of this node so far, opened with the indent and the node's id
Every node starts the same way, so a reader always sees the id first.

Add the fields that the kind of node decides:

name, layer, calls, takes, gives — a block root holds these, because it stands for a whole function of the file.
story — added to a block root only when it has one.
layer — all that a beat node gets, because a beat has no name and no calls.
Add text and lines, the two fields that every node has: what the node says, and the lines of the file it covers.
A node with no children is complete: close the object and give the one line back.

kids = each child written by write_node again, with two more spaces of indent
The node then closes with those children in a children list, so the text keeps the shape of the tree.

map.name: write_map
map.takes: the output path and the map object
map.gives: a JSON file on disk
map.story:
Example: with m["links"] empty, the file holds the line "links": [], not an empty block over three lines.
The text is built by hand, so the layout never changes between runs.
ensure_ascii=False keeps characters like — as themselves. The file ends with one newline.
map.text: write_map(path, m) -> None — writes the finished map to path as JSON, laid out line by line for a person to read

children.text:
rows = the link rows as JSON text, one row per line
links_part = those rows inside brackets, or "[]" when there are no links

One row per line lets a reader scan the links without a formatter.

trows = the term rows as JSON text, one row per line
terms_part = those rows inside brackets, or "[]" when there are no terms
tree = every top-level block as JSON text, from write_node, with its children indented below it
join the file name, the links, the terms and the tree into one string, and write it to path

map.name: compile_block
map.takes: one block, its cells, and the whole file with its statements
map.gives: the checked tree node of the block and the terms its story defines
map.story:
Example: a block of one cell gives a node with no children key.
Each failed try adds its error to errs, so the next prompt lists every rule broken so far. After 8 failed tries the program stops with sys.exit.
map.text: compile_block(bl, cells, name, code, lines, stmts, ess, ctx) -> node, terms — asks claude to explain one block and retries with the broken rules until the answer passes every check

children.text: take one block bl with the cells that belong to it, plus the file text and its statements

bstmts = the statements that sit fully inside the lines of this block
Only these can be cut by a beat, so only these are sent.

stext = the bstmts as line ranges, a child indented under its parent, or an empty string when the block holds no statement
The model needs them because a beat holds all of a statement or none of it.

Two more prompt fields:
label = the function name with "()", or the words for the top-level script code
span = the line ranges of the block, as text

rows = one prompt line for each cell, written by row_of

base = the full prompt, with the file, the label, the span, the ctx of the calls explained already, the cells and their count filled in

Three names hold the state between tries:
note = the extra text put after the prompt when the last answer was bad, empty at the start
errs = every rule broken so far, one line for each
m = the last answer, None before the first try
the block gets at most 8 tries
ask_claude sends the prompt plus the note and gives back the JSON answer, then check_block tests that answer against every rule and raises on the first break

node = the root of the block: its text, takes, gives, story, and the lines of all its cells joined by merge
When the block has more than one cell, each beat becomes a child node at layer 1 with the merged lines of the cells it covers.
print the counts of cells, beats and terms, then give back the node and the terms with their spaces trimmed
a broken rule is not the end: print it, add it to errs, and build note from the last answer, the new error, and the full list of rules broken so far, so the next try repairs the same answer
after 8 bad answers, stop the program with sys.exit and name the block that failed

map.name: main
map.takes: a file path in sys.argv[1]
map.gives: a map.json file next to that source file
map.story:
Example: sys.argv[1] is decompile.py; main() writes map.json in the same folder.
Blocks compile in layer order, so every callee is explained before its caller.
The saved tree goes back to file order.
A term is kept once, from the first block that defines it.
map.text: main() -> None — reads the file named on the command line, explains every block of it, and writes map.json beside it

children.text:
path = the file named on the command line.
src = its text, and lines = that text cut into single lines.
The assert stops an empty file here, before any work starts.

code = the same lines with a number and a bar in front of each one.
This is the form of the file that every prompt shows to claude.

cells = the pieces of the file from cells_of, the smallest parts a beat can name.
stmts = one row per statement with its depth and line range, from statements.

ess = the code lines that hold no smaller statement inside them.
A statement that contains another one is dropped, and blank lines are removed at the end.
The checker needs ess to see whether a beat cuts a statement in half.

Four facts about the blocks of the file:
blocks — one record per def, class or script part, from blocks_of
body — the top-level syntax nodes, empty when the file is not Python
names — the block names that come from a def or a class
calls — for each block, the blocks it calls, from calls_of

lay = a layer number per block from layers_of.
A block always sits above every block it calls.

parts = the cells of each block, kept under the block name.
A cell goes to the one block whose line ranges hold all of it.

Three stores for the run that follows:
done — the finished root of each block, by name
tout — the terms of the whole file, in first-seen order
tseen — the term words taken already, so a word is kept once

Go through the blocks from the lowest layer up, so a callee is done before its caller.

ctx = the one-line meanings of the blocks this block calls, read out of done.
compile_block then asks claude to explain the block and checks the answer.

Each new term joins tout, and the root gets its name, layer, calls and line ranges before it goes into done.

tree = the finished roots, sorted back into file order.
number gives every node an id, and owner_of builds the table from line number to node id.

m = the whole map: the file name, the rows from links, the terms and the tree.
write_map saves it as map.json next to the source file, and the print reports the counts of the run.
